name: HSI (Heaviness of Smoking Index)
seoDesc: HSI (Heaviness of Smoking Index): a free health calculator that walks you through 3 values, with the formula spelled out and a worked example.
summary: The HSI (Heaviness of Smoking Index) calculator returns heaviness of Smoking Index (HSI) from the 2 fields on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below. It suits an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the HSI (Heaviness of Smoking Index) calculator work?
sections.html:
The HSI (Heaviness of Smoking Index) calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports heaviness of Smoking Index (HSI) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
What you supply, field by field
FieldUnits and meaning
How soon after you wake up do you have your first cigarette?pick the option that matches your case — 4 options, such as within 5 min, 6-30 min and 31-60 min. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
How many cigarettes do you typically smoke per day?pick the option that matches your case — 4 options, such as 10 or fewer, 11-20 and 21-30. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the HSI (Heaviness of Smoking Index) calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Heaviness of Smoking Index (HSI)=(how soon after you wake up do you have your first cigarette? + how many cigarettes do you typically smoke per day?)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Open the page and it is already filled in. With the values it starts from — How soon after you wake up do you have your first cigarette? set to Within 5 min and How many cigarettes do you typically smoke per day? set to 10 or fewer — it reports Heaviness of Smoking Index (HSI) = 3.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Heaviness of Smoking Index (HSI) = 3 should be roughly the size you expected from How soon after you wake up do you have your first cigarette? set to Within 5 min and How many cigarettes do you typically smoke per day? set to 10 or fewer.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The HSI (Heaviness of Smoking Index) calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the HSI (Heaviness of Smoking Index) calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The 2 drop-downs on this page offer a fixed list of cases. A value that is not on the list cannot be entered, and the nearest option is not always a good substitute.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — how soon after you wake up do you have your first cigarette? for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What does the HSI (Heaviness of Smoking Index) calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns heaviness of Smoking Index (HSI). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the HSI (Heaviness of Smoking Index) calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Heaviness of Smoking Index (HSI) = 3. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the HSI (Heaviness of Smoking Index) calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
